To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
hassles are related to psychopathology in nonclinical samples, but that the nature and strength of these relations vary widely across different types of hassles.
the HS-R subscales are differentially predictive of psychopathology symptom severity and change in severity over time.
the eight HS-R subscale scores differentially predict psychopatology symptom levels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how life events are associated with psychopathology.
identifying which life event categories predict psychopathology symptoms.
identifying those hassles that are the best predictors of psychopathology levels and/or changes in levels of psychopathology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hassles are associated with psychopathology levels and changes in psychopathological symptom levels.
the ability to predict psychopathological symptom levels is not uniform across all HS-R subscales.
hassles do not predict changes in psychopathological symptom levels over time, and that the ability of hassles to predict levels of psychopathology at a single time point is limited.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HS-R subscales differentially predict psychopathy levels.
the HS-R is a useful measure for predicting psychopathology levels in nonclinical populations, and that the HS-R's subscales should be interpreted with caution.
hassles are a general risk factor for psychopathology, but that the nature of this risk factor is complex and may be influenced by the specific type of hassles that occur.
The main takeaway from our work is that
different types of hassles predict different types of psychopathology.
